paragraphs: When the Sistine ceiling emerged from its cleaning in 1994, a number of art historians objected that something had been lost. The colours were undeniably brighter; what troubled the objectors was the possibility that Michelangelo had intended them not to be. The darkened surface, they argued, was not simply grime but included a layer the painter had applied himself, a final modulation of tone that the solvents had dissolved along with four centuries of candle smoke.

The conservators replied that the evidence for such a layer was thin, and that the preference for the darkened ceiling was a preference formed by habit. Generations had known the frescoes only in their obscured state, had written about them in those terms, and had come to regard the resulting sombreness as part of the work's meaning. On this account the objection was not aesthetic judgement but familiarity mistaken for it.

The exchange is usually reported as a technical dispute, which it was, but underneath it lies a question that no amount of pigment analysis settles. A painting is an object that changes. Varnish yellows, pigments fade, supports warp. If the work is identified with the object as the artist left it, then the conservator's task is restitution, and every intervening change is damage to be reversed where it can be. If the work is instead the object as it has travelled through time, accumulating the marks of its own history, then the cleaning destroys something irreplaceable in pursuit of a state that exists only as an inference.

Neither position survives being held consistently. The restitutionist must concede that there is no moment at which a painting was finished in the relevant sense: artists revised, workshops completed, patrons demanded changes. The state being restored is a reconstruction, and the conservator who claims to be merely uncovering is concealing the extent of their own authorship. But the historicist position is worse off still, for if every change is to be respected, then so is the fire, the flood, the overpainting by a later and lesser hand. A doctrine that cannot distinguish patina from vandalism has given up the ability to say anything at all.

What follows is not that the question is unanswerable but that it is the wrong shape. The conservator is not recovering an original or preserving a history; they are making a decision about what the object will be used for. A painting studied by scholars for evidence of technique has different requirements from the same painting hanging in a church where people pray. The Sistine ceiling is both, which is why the dispute was so bitter and why it could not be resolved by looking harder at the plaster.

This is an uncomfortable conclusion, because it makes conservation a matter of purposes rather than of facts, and purposes are contested in ways that pigment layers are not. It has the advantage of being true to what conservators actually do. Every treatment report records choices that no analysis compelled, and the honest ones say so.

The standard shipping container is a box of corrugated steel with a set of fittings at its corners. It carries no technology that was unavailable in 1900, and the idea of packing goods into a reusable box is older than that. Yet the container is routinely credited with a transformation of world trade more thorough than any machine of the period, and the puzzle of how so unremarkable an object did so much is instructive about where economic change actually comes from.

The answer is not in the box but in everything that had to be rearranged around it. A container is useless unless the crane at the next port can lift it, the chassis at the next terminal can carry it, and the ship it is loaded onto has cells built to its dimensions. Each of those investments is worth making only if the others have been made. The box therefore could not spread the way a better plough spreads, farm by farm, each adopter gaining whether or not the neighbours follow. It had to arrive everywhere at once or very nearly, and the decades between the first container voyage and the system's maturity were spent not on engineering but on arguments about whose dimensions would prevail.

Those arguments were settled by a standards committee, which is why they are seldom told as a story. The settlement imposed real costs: the eventual dimensions suited nobody's existing fleet particularly well, and several operators with better-adapted equipment were made worse off by a decision that served the system. Economists sometimes describe such outcomes as the triumph of the network over its members, which is accurate but can be read as approval. It is worth saying plainly that standardisation redistributed as well as created, and that the losers were not compensated.

What followed is well documented. The cost of moving manufactured goods across an ocean fell by an order of magnitude and then kept falling. Firms that had located near their customers because freight was dear discovered that it no longer was, and the geography of production came apart from the geography of consumption. Ports that could not handle containers lost their traffic to ports that could, often within a decade, and the dockworkers of the old waterfronts lost occupations that had supported their districts for generations.

It is tempting to describe this as the container's doing, and the temptation should be resisted, not because the attribution is false but because it is too easy. The box made a reorganisation possible; it did not decide that the reorganisation would take the form it did. The decisions that determined who gained and who lost were made in committee rooms, union negotiations and port authority budgets, by people who could have decided otherwise. Attributing the outcome to the object removes those people from the account, which is convenient for them and misleading for everyone else.

Two drivers leave the same party equally drunk and drive home by the same route. One arrives without incident. The other, through no difference in skill, attention or intention, rounds a corner at the moment a child steps into the road, and kills her. We do not treat these two people alike. The first is a fool; the second is the subject of a criminal trial, a lifetime of grief, and a judgement that attaches to them permanently. Yet the only difference between them is where a child happened to be standing.

The difficulty this raises is not a puzzle about the law, which has its own reasons for attending to outcomes. It is a puzzle about moral judgement itself, and it is sharp because two principles we hold firmly turn out to conflict. The first is that people are responsible only for what lies within their control. The second is that the driver who killed a child did something terrible, and that someone who denied this would be missing something rather than merely disagreeing.

The tempting move is to keep the first principle and treat the second as an error: the two drivers are equally culpable, and our harsher response to the second is a superstition we would do better to outgrow, like blaming the messenger. This is tidy, and it fails to survive contact with what the second driver feels. The appropriate response of someone who has killed a child is not the relief of recognising that they were no worse than their luckier friend. A person who reasoned their way to that relief would strike us as having understood the argument and missed the event.

Nor can the problem be confined to outcomes. The driver's circumstances were also a matter of luck: that a party was held, that they were invited, that the route home passed a street where children play. So was their character, which was formed by an upbringing they did not choose, in a society whose norms about drinking they absorbed before they could evaluate them. Once luck in circumstance and luck in constitution are admitted, the domain genuinely within a person's control shrinks toward nothing, and with it the domain of moral judgement.

A philosopher who follows the argument to that conclusion has proved too much, and the proper response is not to accept it but to suspect the principle that generated it. Perhaps the demand that responsibility track control is not a discovery about morality but an aspiration within it, one we apply in some contexts and suspend in others without inconsistency, because moral judgement was never a single thing with a single logic.

That suggestion will satisfy nobody who wants morality to be systematic. Its merit is that it describes what we actually do. We hold the unlucky driver responsible and we also know that they were unlucky, and we manage to do both without the sky falling in. A theory that cannot accommodate this is a theory that has decided in advance what morality must be like, and is correcting the phenomena to suit.

A dictionary looks like a record of what words mean, and lexicographers are at pains to insist that this is what it is. They describe rather than prescribe; they report usage rather than licensing it. The insistence is sincere, and it is also incomplete, because a dictionary is not a transcript. Someone decides which words are entered, and in what order the senses are listed, and where a usage is marked as informal or offensive or obsolete. Each of those decisions is a judgement, and the sum of them is an account of the language that no speaker of it would recognise as merely descriptive.

Consider the ordering of senses. A word that has drifted may be given its oldest meaning first, on historical principles, or its commonest meaning first, on the principle that a reader wants the likely answer soonest. Neither ordering is wrong, and the choice between them determines what a user takes the word to mean, since few read past the first entry. A dictionary organised historically will tell a reader that to decimate is to destroy a tenth; one organised by frequency will tell them it is to destroy a great part. Both are reports of usage. They are reports of different usages, selected by a rule the reader never sees.

The labels are harder still. To mark a usage as informal is to make a claim about the situations in which it would be noticed, which varies by region, age and class in ways no single label can hold. To mark one as offensive is to take a side in a dispute among speakers, some of whom use the word without offence and some of whom are injured by it. Lexicographers have become careful here, and their carefulness takes the form of longer notes rather than of fewer judgements.

None of this is an argument against dictionaries, and it would be a poor reader who concluded that the enterprise is arbitrary. The alternative to a judgement is not neutrality but a different judgement, usually a worse one made less deliberately. The point is narrower: the claim to be merely describing does real work in a dictionary's authority, and that claim cannot be fully true of any book that must decide what to put first.

There is a practical reason the profession resists this. A dictionary that advertised its judgements would invite argument about each of them, and the labour of lexicography is already greater than its funding. The appearance of neutrality is partly a defence against being asked to justify ten thousand decisions to people with strong views about a dozen of them. That is an understandable position and not quite an honest one, and the better dictionaries have begun to say so in their front matter, where almost nobody looks.

Western musical notation is often described as a recording technology, a means of fixing sound so that it survives its performance. The description is natural and it inverts the history. Notation did not begin as a way of preserving music that already existed in finished form; it began as a set of reminders for singers who knew the music already, marks that indicated the shape of a melody without specifying its pitches, useless to anyone who had not learned the chant by ear. What notation preserved, at first, was not the music but the memory of someone who had it.

The gradual specification of pitch, and much later of duration, changed what the marks could do, and changed with it the relationship between composer and performer. A score that fixes every pitch and every value can be realised by a musician who has never heard the piece. This is an extraordinary achievement and it carries a cost that is seldom counted: the more a notation specifies, the more it implies that what it does not specify is unimportant. Phrasing, articulation, the thousand decisions that distinguish one performance from another, came to be regarded as matters of interpretation, a category that did not exist when the marks were reminders and everything was interpretation.

Traditions that developed other solutions make the point sharply. In classical Indian music the raga is transmitted by a teacher to a student over years, and what is transmitted is not a sequence of notes but a set of possibilities, constraints and characteristic gestures from which a performance is assembled in the moment. A transcription of a performance records what one musician did once, and a student who learned from such a transcription would have learned a performance rather than the raga. The notation is possible; it is simply not the thing.

It would be a mistake to conclude that Western notation impoverished the music written in it. What it did was redistribute. Decisions that had belonged to the performer migrated to the composer, and the kind of complexity a composer could demand grew far beyond what an ensemble could have held in memory. A late symphony is not a transcription of something that could have been improvised. It exists because the notation exists.

The question worth asking is therefore not whether notation gained or lost but what it made invisible. A musician trained to read will hear a performance as a realisation of a text and will evaluate it against that text. A musician trained in a transmitted tradition will hear the same performance as an instance of a practice, and will ask a different question about it, one for which the score provides no evidence at all.

Historians are trained to be sceptical of their sources, and the training concentrates on a particular kind of scepticism: whether a document is authentic, whether its author was in a position to know, whether an interest distorted what was recorded. These are the right questions and they share an assumption, which is that the document exists. The harder problem is the one the training does not reach, because it concerns the documents that were never made.

An archive is not a sample of the past. It is the residue of institutions that kept records for their own purposes, and those purposes determined what was worth writing down. A medieval manor recorded what it was owed, so we know a great deal about rents and almost nothing about what tenants said to one another. A colonial administration recorded what it taxed and what it punished, so the colonised appear in the record overwhelmingly as debtors and defendants. The silences are not gaps in an otherwise complete account; they are the shape of the account, and a historian who treats the archive as a sample will reproduce the institution's priorities while believing they are reporting the past.

The standard remedy is to read against the grain: to take a document made for one purpose and extract from it something its makers did not intend to record. A court record of a prosecution for unlicensed brewing tells us that women brewed and sold ale, which the court did not set out to establish. This technique is indispensable and it has a limit that its practitioners sometimes forget. Reading against the grain can only recover what left a trace in some record, however oblique. A practice that no institution had reason to notice leaves no oblique trace either, and the historian who has become skilled at the technique may come to feel that nothing is beyond recovery.

There is a temptation to fill such silences by inference, reasoning from what is known elsewhere to what must have been the case here. The temptation should be resisted in proportion to its usefulness. Inference of this kind is sometimes the only route to a claim worth making, and it produces an account that reads exactly like an account built from evidence, since the prose is the same. The honest practice is to mark the inference as what it is, which historians do unevenly, and which readers outside the discipline are poorly placed to detect.

What follows is not that history is unreliable. It is that the confidence appropriate to a historical claim depends on something the claim itself does not display: whether the records that would have contradicted it could have survived. A statement about medieval rents rests on documents an institution had every reason to keep accurate. A statement about medieval belief rests on documents that mention belief incidentally, if at all. Those two statements may be written in the same tone, and should not be read in the same way.

Travel writers are fond of distinguishing the pilgrim from the tourist. The pilgrim travels toward something that matters; the tourist consumes places. The distinction flatters whoever is drawing it, which is reason enough to examine it, and it does not survive much contact with the history of either practice.

Medieval pilgrimage routes were commercial enterprises. They had inns, guides, souvenir trades and a well-developed market in forged relics. Pilgrims complained about prices, collected badges proving where they had been, and travelled in groups organised for the purpose by people who made a living from it. A modern tourist who bought a mass-produced object at a famous site, grumbled about the cost and photographed themselves beside the monument would have been entirely legible to a fourteenth-century traveller, who did the same things with different technology.

There is a further resemblance that the writers tend to pass over. Both practices generate an anxiety about authenticity, and both resolve it the same way. The medieval traveller worried that the relic was forged and that the guide was fleecing them, and sought out the obscure shrine on the assumption that obscurity was evidence of genuineness. The modern traveller performs the identical manoeuvre, avoiding the crowded site in favour of one that fewer people have reached, and treating scarcity of visitors as a proxy for something it has never reliably indicated. The anxiety is not a symptom of shallow tourism. It is what happens whenever a person travels a long way on the strength of a claim they cannot check.

The usual rescue of the distinction is to locate it in the traveller's inner state rather than their behaviour. The pilgrim seeks transformation; the tourist seeks diversion. This is harder to refute because it is harder to observe, which is not a point in its favour. It also assumes a uniformity within each category that neither has. Some medieval pilgrims went because they were sentenced to; some went to escape a marriage; some went because their neighbours were going. Some modern tourists stand in front of a painting and are changed by it.

A more defensible version of the distinction concerns not the traveller but the destination, and specifically whether the place makes a claim on the visitor. A shrine asserts that something happened there which ought to alter the person standing in front of it. A beach asserts nothing. A traveller may decline the shrine's claim, and many do, but the claim is made by the site rather than brought to it, and that is a real difference between kinds of place rather than a flattering story about kinds of people.

This reframing has a consequence the writers who prefer the original distinction may not welcome. Many of the destinations they would class as touristic do make such claims: a battlefield, a preserved camp, the house where a writer worked. These sites assert that what happened there should change the visitor, and they are visited by people in shorts carrying cameras, who are frequently changed. If the distinction is about the claim a place makes, then the pilgrim is not a rarer figure than the tourist. The pilgrim is most of the tourists, some of the time.

A citizens' assembly selects a few dozen people at random from the population, pays them to spend some days learning about a contested question from experts chosen for balance, has them deliberate under a facilitator, and asks them to produce a recommendation. Assemblies of this kind have been convened on constitutional questions, climate policy and assisted dying, and their advocates make a claim that deserves examination: that the resulting recommendation has a legitimacy that a poll of the same population would not.

The claim is not that the assembly is more representative. A random sample of forty is statistically worse than a poll of two thousand, and advocates know this. The claim concerns what the sample has done. A polled citizen answers from whatever they happen to think on a Tuesday evening; an assembly member answers after days of evidence and argument with people who disagree. The output is held to be not merely a different opinion but a better-founded one, the view the public would hold if the public had the time.

This is a strong claim and the honest version of it is conditional. It holds only if the process does what it says. If the experts are not balanced, the assembly launders a predetermined conclusion through forty ordinary people, and does so more effectively than a government could have asserted it directly, because the recommendation now carries the authority of the public. If the facilitation steers, the same. The mechanism that gives the assembly its legitimacy is invisible to those who receive its output, which means the output cannot be assessed by its recipients.

Critics usually press a different objection: that the assembly's members are unaccountable, having been chosen by lot and answerable to nobody. This objection is weaker than it looks. Accountability matters for those who exercise power continuously and can be removed, and an assembly that meets for six days and then dissolves exercises no power at all unless a legislature adopts its recommendation. The members propose; others dispose, and those others remain accountable in the ordinary way.

A second reply to the critics is worth recording because it cuts both ways. Assemblies are frequently convened on precisely the questions that elected politicians have found impossible to settle, which suggests they are valued less for the quality of their deliberation than for their capacity to absorb a decision nobody wishes to own. On that reading the assembly is not a supplement to representative politics but a relief valve for it, and a legislature that routinely refers its hardest questions elsewhere has not become more deliberative. It has found a way of appearing to decide.

The sharper worry is about what the assembly does to the arguments it was convened to settle. A question sent to an assembly is removed from ordinary politics for the duration and returned with a recommendation that is difficult to oppose without appearing to oppose the public itself. That is precisely the point for those who convene them, and it should give pause even to those sympathetic to the outcomes. A procedure that makes a conclusion hard to argue with has not thereby made it correct, and a democracy that cannot distinguish between the two has acquired an expensive way of ending conversations.

A narrator is called unreliable when the reader is given grounds to doubt their account. The definition is serviceable and it conceals a difficulty, because grounds to doubt must come from somewhere, and in a first-person narrative there is nothing in the text that does not pass through the narrator. The reader who concludes that a narrator is lying has done so using evidence the liar supplied.

The usual explanation is that the author plants signals over the narrator's head: a detail the narrator reports without understanding, a judgement that the surrounding facts do not support, a gap where an explanation should be. This is right as far as it goes, and it describes a technique that depends entirely on the reader noticing. A signal that is missed is not a signal. An unreliable narrator is therefore not a property of a text but a relation between a text and a reader, and the same novel will have an unreliable narrator for one reader and a straightforward one for another.

The point is easier to see in borderline cases than in flagrant ones. A narrator who describes a childhood as happy, in sentences that record a series of events a reader would call neglect, has not said anything false. The reader who notices the mismatch and the reader who does not have both read every word on the page, and nothing in the text announces which of them has read it correctly. The difference lies in what each brought to the sentences, and no amount of rereading settles it, because rereading supplies no evidence the first reading lacked.

This has an awkward consequence for criticism, which likes to settle such questions. If a reader finishes a novel believing the narrator, it is not obvious what would show them wrong. One can point to the planted details, and the reader can accept them and still accept the narrator's gloss, since the gloss was designed to accommodate them. Critics in this position often fall back on authorial intention, which is a retreat from the text to something outside it, and one that most of the same critics would refuse in other arguments.

There is a better response available, which is to stop treating reliability as a verdict and treat it as a reading. A reading is defended by showing what it makes available: what the novel becomes if the narrator is doubted, which details acquire significance, which silences begin to look deliberate. A reading that illuminates more of the book is better than one that illuminates less, and that comparison can be made without appealing to what the author wanted or declaring the other reader mistaken.

The cost of this approach is that it gives up a kind of certainty that critics have been reluctant to surrender, and the reluctance is understandable. It is one thing to say that a novel supports two readings; it is another to say that a novel in which the narrator murders someone and does not mention it supports a reading in which nothing happened. But the test survives the hard case. The reading in which nothing happened leaves a great deal of the book inert, and that is the ground on which it fails. It fails as a reading, which is the only way a reading can fail.

questions.stem: The main idea of the passage is that:

choices.A: the cleaning of the Sistine ceiling destroyed a layer applied by Michelangelo himself
choices.B: conservators should defer to art historians when the two disagree about a treatment
choices.C: paintings cannot be meaningfully restored because no original state can be identified
choices.D: disputes about restoration turn on what the restored object is to be used for, not on facts about it

questions.explanation: The author sets up the two standard positions, shows that neither survives being held consistently, and then argues that the question is 'the wrong shape': conservation is 'a matter of purposes rather than of facts'. That is the conclusion the whole passage is built toward.

wrong.A: The author treats this as the objectors' claim and reports that the conservators found the evidence for it thin. It is a detail in the argument, not its point.
wrong.B: The passage never recommends that either group defer to the other; it says the dispute could not be settled by looking harder at the evidence at all.
wrong.C: The author grants that restoration involves reconstruction but explicitly denies that the question is unanswerable, calling it instead badly posed.

questions.stem: The author characterises the objectors' preference for the darkened ceiling as possibly:

choices.A: a judgement based on documentary evidence about Michelangelo's methods
choices.B: a deliberate attempt to discredit the conservators
choices.C: habituation to a familiar appearance, mistaken for aesthetic judgement
choices.D: an application of the principle that every change should be respected

questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives the conservators' reply directly: the preference was 'formed by habit', generations having known the work only in its obscured state, so the objection was 'familiarity mistaken for' aesthetic judgement.

wrong.A: The conservators' reply was precisely that the documentary and physical evidence for the extra layer was thin.
wrong.B: Nothing in the passage attributes bad faith to anyone; the dispute is presented as a genuine disagreement.
wrong.D: That principle is introduced later as the historicist position, and is not what the second paragraph attributes to the objectors.

questions.stem: The author's objection to the historicist position is that it:

choices.A: relies on an inference about a state of the object that no longer exists
choices.B: underestimates how much pigments fade over four centuries
choices.C: requires conservators to conceal the extent of their own authorship
choices.D: cannot distinguish between damage worth respecting and damage worth reversing

questions.explanation: The author grants the historicist case and then presses it: if every change is to be respected, so are the fire, the flood and the later overpainting. 'A doctrine that cannot distinguish patina from vandalism has given up the ability to say anything at all.'

wrong.A: This is the objection raised against the restitutionist position, not the historicist one.
wrong.B: The fading of pigments is offered as background about how objects change, not as a flaw in either position.
wrong.C: Concealed authorship is charged against the conservator who claims merely to be uncovering, which is the restitutionist's error.

questions.stem: The author's claim that the restored state is 'a reconstruction' functions in the argument primarily to:

choices.A: show that the conservators acted improperly in cleaning the ceiling
choices.B: establish that scientific analysis is unreliable in conservation
choices.C: undermine the restitutionist's claim to be merely uncovering what was there
choices.D: support the view that the darkened ceiling should have been preserved

questions.explanation: The sentence sits inside the critique of the restitutionist position and leads directly to the charge that such a conservator 'is concealing the extent of their own authorship'. Its work is to deny that restoration is a neutral act of recovery.

wrong.A: The author reaches no verdict on the Sistine cleaning, and the same paragraph goes on to treat the opposing position as worse off.
wrong.B: The passage relies on analysis as evidence - it reports that the evidence for the extra layer was thin - and never calls it unreliable.
wrong.D: The author declines to endorse preserving the darkened state, dismantling the position that would require it.

questions.stem: A museum proposes to clean a medieval altarpiece that is still used in weekly worship at the church that owns it. Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that the decision should turn on:

choices.A: whether chemical analysis can establish the altarpiece's original appearance
choices.B: whether the congregation or the museum's scholars have the stronger claim to the object
choices.C: whether the accumulated changes count as patina rather than as damage
choices.D: what the altarpiece is to be used for, which may differ between the two

questions.explanation: The author's conclusion is that the conservator is 'making a decision about what the object will be used for', and the passage names exactly this tension: a painting studied for technique has different requirements from one hanging where people pray.

wrong.A: The author argues that no amount of analysis settles the question, which is why the dispute over the ceiling could not be resolved by looking harder at the plaster.
wrong.B: The passage frames the issue as one of purposes rather than of competing claims of ownership or authority.
wrong.C: The patina-and-vandalism distinction is raised to defeat the historicist position, not offered as the test to apply.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's conclusion?

choices.A: Conservators routinely disagree about what a given object should be used for
choices.B: A majority of art historians came to accept the cleaned ceiling within a decade
choices.C: Chemical analysis can now establish with certainty which layers an artist applied
choices.D: Some paintings have been so altered that no original state can be inferred at all

questions.explanation: The conclusion is that the dispute is about purposes rather than facts, and that no amount of evidence settles it. If analysis could establish with certainty which layers were the artist's own, the restitutionist would have the factual answer the author says is unavailable, and the disagreement would become tractable on the author's own terms.

wrong.A: Disagreement about purposes is consistent with the author's view and is in fact predicted by it; the author calls purposes 'contested in ways that pigment layers are not'.
wrong.B: Later acceptance speaks to the conservators' judgement about one object and leaves the author's account of what conservation involves untouched.
wrong.D: This strengthens the author, by reinforcing that the restored state is an inference rather than a recovered fact.

questions.stem: The author's central point about the shipping container is that:

choices.A: its effects are better explained by the decisions made around it than by the object itself
choices.B: it required technology that only became available in the second half of the twentieth century
choices.C: its benefits were outweighed by the costs imposed on dockworkers and smaller ports
choices.D: standards committees are the primary engine of economic change

questions.explanation: The passage opens by noting that the box used no new technology, spends its length on the coordination and bargaining that had to happen around it, and closes by insisting that attributing the outcome to the object 'removes those people from the account'.

wrong.B: The first paragraph says the opposite: the container 'carries no technology that was unavailable in 1900'.
wrong.C: The author records the losses carefully but never weighs them against the gains or declares a net verdict.
wrong.D: The committee matters in this case, but the author's argument is about decisions generally - unions and port budgets are named alongside it.

questions.stem: The comparison between the container and 'a better plough' is used to illustrate that the container:

choices.A: was less sophisticated than agricultural machinery of the same era
choices.B: spread more slowly than innovations in farming had
choices.C: required skilled operators in a way that simpler tools did not
choices.D: could not deliver benefits to an adopter acting alone

questions.explanation: The plough is introduced precisely for the contrast: it spreads 'farm by farm, each adopter gaining whether or not the neighbours follow', whereas the container needed cranes, chassis and ships to match, so it 'had to arrive everywhere at once or very nearly'.

wrong.A: The passage makes no claim about the relative sophistication of the two, only about how each spreads.
wrong.B: Speed of diffusion is a consequence of the point, not the point. The comparison is about whether a lone adopter gains.
wrong.C: Skill is never mentioned in the comparison or anywhere else in the passage.

questions.stem: The author's remark that the economists' description 'can be read as approval' suggests that the author:

choices.A: believes economists deliberately conceal the costs of standardisation
choices.B: regards the phrase as inaccurate as a description of what happened
choices.C: thinks an accurate description may still obscure who was harmed
choices.D: doubts that the network as a whole gained from the settlement

questions.explanation: The author calls the description 'accurate' in the same sentence, then immediately insists it is 'worth saying plainly' that standardisation redistributed and that the losers went uncompensated. The worry is about what an accurate phrase lets a reader pass over.

wrong.A: Deliberate concealment is a stronger charge than the text supports; the author objects to how a phrase reads, not to anyone's motives.
wrong.B: The author explicitly grants that the description is accurate.
wrong.D: The gain to the network is not in dispute; the author's concern is its distribution.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following would the author most likely consider a comparable case?

choices.A: A country adopting a rail gauge incompatible with its neighbours' and later changing it
choices.B: A pharmaceutical company developing a drug that treats a previously untreatable disease
choices.C: A manufacturer improving the fuel efficiency of its own delivery vehicles
choices.D: A city replacing its bus fleet with newer models of the same design

questions.explanation: The author's case is about a technology whose value depends on everyone adopting the same specification, and about the costs imposed when a standard is settled. A rail gauge is the same problem: incompatible gauges strand traffic, and converting imposes costs on whoever has to change.

wrong.B: A drug benefits its user regardless of what anyone else adopts, which is the plough case rather than the container case.
wrong.C: A firm improving its own vehicles gains alone, with no coordination required.
wrong.D: Replacing like with like involves no standard to settle and no one made worse off by someone else's decision.

questions.stem:
The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about technological change?

I. It is driven primarily by the intrinsic properties of new inventions
II. Accounts that credit objects for outcomes can serve the interests of decision-makers
III. Its distributional consequences follow necessarily from the technology adopted

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: II and III only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Only the second is the author's view, and the closing sentence states it: attributing the outcome to the object 'removes those people from the account, which is convenient for them'. The first is what the passage argues against from its opening observation that the box used no new technology. The third is denied by the insistence that the decision-makers 'could have decided otherwise'.

wrong.A: The first statement is the view the passage was written to refute, beginning from the point that the container used no technology unavailable in 1900.
wrong.C: The second belongs, but the third does not: the author insists the outcome was decided by people who could have decided otherwise.
wrong.D: This includes both statements the author rejects, leaving only the middle one defensible.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the standards settlement is best described as:

choices.A: approving of its efficiency while noting that its costs fell unevenly
choices.B: critical of the committee for choosing dimensions that suited nobody
choices.C: indifferent, since the outcome was determined by the technology
choices.D: regretful that the settlement was reached at all

questions.explanation: The author accepts that the settlement 'served the system' and that enormous gains followed, while pressing that it 'redistributed as well as created, and that the losers were not compensated'. That is acknowledgement of the benefit with insistence on the cost.

wrong.B: The author reports that the dimensions suited nobody's existing fleet as a fact about the settlement, not as a failing of the committee.
wrong.C: The closing paragraph denies that the technology determined the outcome, and the tone throughout is anything but indifferent.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests the author would prefer no settlement; the complaint is about uncompensated losers.

questions.stem: The two drivers are introduced in order to:

choices.A: argue that criminal law attends too much to outcomes
choices.B: demonstrate that drunk driving is judged too leniently
choices.C: illustrate how upbringing shapes a person's character
choices.D: show that two principles about moral judgement conflict

questions.explanation: The second paragraph says so directly: the puzzle 'is sharp because two principles we hold firmly turn out to conflict' - that responsibility tracks control, and that the driver who killed a child did something terrible.

wrong.A: The author sets the law aside explicitly, saying it 'has its own reasons for attending to outcomes'.
wrong.B: The passage takes no position on the severity of drink-driving penalties.
wrong.C: Luck in constitution appears later as an extension of the problem, not as the point of the opening example.

questions.stem: The author rejects the 'tempting move' chiefly because it:

choices.A: conflicts with the principle that responsibility requires control
choices.B: relies on an analogy with blaming the messenger that does not hold
choices.C: cannot account for what the driver who killed a child ought to feel
choices.D: has been refuted by the law's treatment of comparable cases

questions.explanation: The objection is given in full: the move 'fails to survive contact with what the second driver feels', and someone who reasoned their way to relief would have 'understood the argument and missed the event'.

wrong.A: The tempting move preserves that principle; it is the second principle it sacrifices.
wrong.B: The messenger comparison is the author's own shorthand for the view being described, and is not examined or refuted.
wrong.D: The author has already set the law aside as irrelevant to the moral puzzle.

questions.stem: In saying that a philosopher who reaches the sceptical conclusion 'has proved too much', the author means that:

choices.A: the argument's conclusion is so extreme that the principle behind it should be doubted
choices.B: the argument contains a formal error that careful reasoning would expose
choices.C: the conclusion is correct but too discouraging to be useful
choices.D: philosophers tend to overstate their findings

questions.explanation: The next clause makes the move explicit: 'the proper response is not to accept it but to suspect the principle that generated it'. An argument that eliminates moral judgement altogether is being treated as evidence against its own premise.

wrong.B: The author never alleges a formal error, and indeed follows the reasoning as valid from its premise.
wrong.C: The author does not grant the conclusion; the whole point is to reject it by rejecting the premise.
wrong.D: No general claim about philosophers' habits is made.

questions.stem: The author's final position is best described as holding that moral judgement:

choices.A: must be made consistent before it can be relied upon
choices.B: should be abandoned in cases where luck plays a substantial role
choices.C: is not a single practice governed by one principle
choices.D: depends ultimately on the consequences of an action

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph proposes that the control principle is 'an aspiration within' morality rather than a discovery about it, applied in some contexts and suspended in others 'without inconsistency, because moral judgement was never a single thing with a single logic'.

wrong.A: The author argues the reverse, closing against theories that correct the phenomena to suit a demand for system.
wrong.B: The author holds the unlucky driver responsible while acknowledging the luck, rather than suspending judgement.
wrong.D: Outcomes matter on this account, but the author also insists that circumstance and character involve luck, so consequences alone are not the ground.

questions.stem: Suppose a surgeon makes a defensible judgement during an operation and the patient dies, while a colleague makes the same judgement in a similar case and the patient lives. The author would most likely say that:

choices.A: holding the first surgeon to a harsher judgement while recognising the bad luck is not inconsistent
choices.B: the two surgeons are equally culpable, and treating them differently is superstition
choices.C: neither surgeon can be judged, since the outcome lay outside their control
choices.D: the case differs from the drivers because professional standards govern it

questions.explanation: This is the author's position applied: 'We hold the unlucky driver responsible and we also know that they were unlucky, and we manage to do both without the sky falling in.' The passage treats that combination as what we actually do rather than as an error.

wrong.B: This is the tempting move the author rejects for failing to survive contact with what the unlucky party feels.
wrong.C: This is the sceptical conclusion the author says proves too much.
wrong.D: Professional standards are never raised, and the author's argument is about moral judgement in general rather than about regulated occupations.

questions.stem: The author's closing charge against a theory that 'cannot accommodate this' is that such a theory:

choices.A: fails to distinguish between legal and moral responsibility
choices.B: ignores the role of luck in forming a person's character
choices.C: is insufficiently rigorous in its treatment of control
choices.D: adjusts the evidence to fit a prior conviction about morality's form

questions.explanation: The last sentence states it: such a theory 'has decided in advance what morality must be like, and is correcting the phenomena to suit'. The complaint is about method - fitting the facts to the theory rather than the reverse.

wrong.A: The legal distinction was set aside in the second paragraph and plays no part in the closing argument.
wrong.B: Luck in character is part of the author's own case, and a systematic theory could acknowledge it.
wrong.C: The author's complaint is not that such theories are insufficiently rigorous but that their rigour is misapplied.

questions.stem: The author's main claim about dictionaries is that they:

choices.A: should abandon the attempt to describe usage and prescribe it openly
choices.B: are arbitrary in their treatment of contested words
choices.C: have become less reliable as labelling practices have changed
choices.D: cannot be purely descriptive, because their structure requires judgements

questions.explanation: The argument runs from the observation that a dictionary 'is not a transcript' to the conclusion that the claim to be merely describing 'cannot be fully true of any book that must decide what to put first'.

wrong.A: The author never recommends prescription and treats the descriptive aim as sincere.
wrong.B: The fourth paragraph rejects this explicitly: 'it would be a poor reader who concluded that the enterprise is arbitrary'.
wrong.C: Labelling practice is said to have become more careful, and no decline in reliability is claimed.

questions.stem: The example of 'decimate' is used to show that:

choices.A: ordering senses by a rule the reader cannot see shapes what the word is taken to mean
choices.B: historical principles of ordering are more accurate than frequency-based ones
choices.C: words with military origins are especially prone to drift
choices.D: readers should be encouraged to read every sense before deciding

questions.explanation: The example sits inside the discussion of sense ordering, and the paragraph closes on exactly this: both are reports of usage, but 'reports of different usages, selected by a rule the reader never sees'.

wrong.B: The author says plainly that 'neither ordering is wrong'.
wrong.C: The word's origin is mentioned only to explain the older sense; no general claim about military vocabulary is made.
wrong.D: The author notes that few read past the first entry as a fact about readers, not as a failing to correct.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward lexicographers is best described as:

choices.A: dismissive of a profession that conceals its methods
choices.B: admiring of their recent progress in labelling contested words
choices.C: neutral, reporting the practice without evaluating it
choices.D: sympathetic to their position while unconvinced by their claim to neutrality

questions.explanation: The author calls the insistence 'sincere', accepts the funding pressure as 'an understandable position', and still concludes that it is 'not quite an honest one'. Sympathy and disagreement at once.

wrong.A: The author defends the enterprise against the charge of arbitrariness and credits the better dictionaries with disclosure.
wrong.B: Greater care in labelling is noted, but the author immediately observes it produces longer notes rather than fewer judgements.
wrong.C: The passage evaluates throughout, ending with a judgement about honesty.

questions.stem: A scientific journal states that it publishes on merit alone, while an editor decides which submissions are sent out for review at all. Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that:

choices.A: the journal's claim is false, since selection cannot be a matter of merit
choices.B: the editor's selection is a judgement that the claim to neutrality conceals
choices.C: the journal's authority would be unaffected if the selection were disclosed
choices.D: the guidelines should be relocated to where authors are more likely to read them

questions.explanation: The author's case is that a claim to neutrality does real work in a reference work's authority while its structure consists of judgements the reader never sees. A journal that advertises merit alone while an editor filters submissions is the same shape, and the author is careful that this is not an accusation of arbitrariness.

wrong.A: The author rejects exactly this inference about dictionaries: 'it would be a poor reader who concluded that the enterprise is arbitrary'. A judgement is not the absence of merit.
wrong.C: The passage says the claim to neutrality 'does real work in a dictionary's authority', so disclosing the judgements would cost something rather than nothing.
wrong.D: The front-matter remark notes where disclosure goes unread; the author draws no recommendation about relocating it, and the point is about the claim rather than its placement.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is most analogous to the author's account of lexicography?

choices.A: A translator who renders a poem freely and says so in a preface
choices.B: A scientist who reports an unexpected result without explaining it
choices.C: A journalist who publishes a correction after an error is pointed out
choices.D: A museum curator who selects and arranges objects while presenting the display as a neutral survey

questions.explanation: The author's case is an enterprise whose authority rests on a claim to neutrality, while its structure - what is included, what comes first, how things are labelled - consists of judgements the audience does not see. A curated display presented as a neutral survey is the same shape.

wrong.A: The translator discloses the judgement rather than presenting the work as neutral, which is the opposite of the pattern described.
wrong.B: Withholding an explanation is not the same as making selective judgements while claiming not to.
wrong.C: Correcting an error concerns accuracy after the fact, not the hidden structure of the work.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that the appearance of neutrality in a reference work:

choices.A: can be defended on practical grounds while remaining misleading
choices.B: is a necessary condition of its usefulness to readers
choices.C: should be abandoned whenever a judgement has been made
choices.D: matters less than the accuracy of the individual entries

questions.explanation: The final paragraph grants a practical defence - the labour exceeds the funding, and neutrality shields the work from endless argument - and then refuses to let the defence settle the matter, calling the position 'understandable' but 'not quite an honest one'.

wrong.B: The author never claims the appearance is necessary, only that it 'does real work in a dictionary's authority'.
wrong.C: That would require abandoning it everywhere, since judgements run through the whole book; the author makes no such demand.
wrong.D: The argument is precisely that structural choices matter alongside the accuracy of entries.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the earliest Western notation:

choices.A: specified pitch but not duration
choices.B: served as a reminder for singers who already knew the music
choices.C: was developed to allow music to be performed by strangers
choices.D: was adapted from systems used in other musical traditions

questions.explanation: The first paragraph states it directly: the marks 'indicated the shape of a melody without specifying its pitches, useless to anyone who had not learned the chant by ear'.

wrong.A: Pitch came later - the passage describes 'the gradual specification of pitch, and much later of duration'.
wrong.C: Performance by a musician who has never heard the piece is presented as a later consequence, not an original aim.
wrong.D: Other traditions are discussed as contrasts; no borrowing is described.

questions.stem:
According to the passage, increasing the specificity of a notation has which of the following consequences?

I. It implies that whatever is left unspecified is unimportant
II. It allows a musician who has never heard a piece to perform it
III. It reduces the complexity a composer can demand

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: I and II only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: The first and second are both in the second paragraph: a score fixing every pitch and value 'can be realised by a musician who has never heard the piece', and the cost is that the more a notation specifies, 'the more it implies that what it does not specify is unimportant'. The third reverses the passage, which says the complexity a composer could demand 'grew far beyond what an ensemble could have held in memory'.

wrong.A: The first holds, but so does the second, which the passage calls 'an extraordinary achievement'.
wrong.B: The second holds, but the passage treats the first as the cost that accompanies it.
wrong.D: This includes the third, which inverts the passage: notation increased the complexity available to composers.

questions.stem: The discussion of the raga serves mainly to:

choices.A: show that some musical knowledge is not the kind of thing a score can carry
choices.B: argue that oral transmission produces better musicians than notation does
choices.C: establish that Indian classical music cannot be written down
choices.D: suggest that Western composers should study transmitted traditions

questions.explanation: The author grants that transcription is possible and then draws the distinction that matters: a transcription 'records what one musician did once', so a student would learn a performance rather than the raga. 'The notation is possible; it is simply not the thing.'

wrong.B: No comparison of musicians' quality is offered anywhere in the passage.
wrong.C: The passage says the opposite in as many words: the notation is possible.
wrong.D: No recommendation is made to composers.

questions.stem: The author's claim that notation 'redistributed' rather than impoverished is best supported by which observation from the passage?

choices.A: Early notation was useless to those who did not know the chant
choices.B: The raga is transmitted over years by a teacher
choices.C: Phrasing and articulation came to be called interpretation
choices.D: A late symphony exists because the notation exists

questions.explanation: Redistribution means decisions moved from performer to composer, and that something became possible that was not possible before. The symphony is the author's instance of the gain side of that trade: it 'is not a transcription of something that could have been improvised'.

wrong.A: This describes notation before the change and so cannot show what the change produced.
wrong.B: This belongs to the contrasting tradition and illustrates what notation cannot carry.
wrong.C: This is the loss side of the trade; redistribution requires showing the gain as well.

questions.stem: Based on the final paragraph, a reader trained in a transmitted tradition hearing an unfamiliar performance would be most likely to ask:

choices.A: whether the performance belongs to the practice it claims to come from
choices.B: whether the performer executed the written text accurately
choices.C: whether the composer's intentions can be recovered from the score
choices.D: whether the notation used was specific enough to be reliable

questions.explanation: The closing sentences contrast a listener who hears a performance 'as a realisation of a text' and evaluates it against that text with one who hears it 'as an instance of a practice' and asks a question 'for which the score provides no evidence at all'.

wrong.B: That is explicitly the question the reading-trained musician asks.
wrong.C: Recovering the composer's intention is still a text-centred question.
wrong.D: The adequacy of the notation is not what either listener is said to ask about.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most CHALLENGE the author's account of what notation made invisible?

choices.A: Some composers write detailed performance instructions alongside the notes
choices.B: Performers trained to read routinely disagree about how a score should sound
choices.C: Transmitted traditions sometimes adopt notation for teaching beginners
choices.D: Early chant notation varied considerably between monasteries

questions.explanation: The author's case is that specification made the unspecified seem unimportant and reduced it to a secondary category. Readers who routinely and substantively disagree about how a score should sound would show that those decisions remain live and contested among exactly the musicians the author says were trained out of them.

wrong.A: Instructions are more specification, which is the trend the author describes rather than a challenge to it.
wrong.C: Adoption for teaching beginners is consistent with the author's view that notation is possible but not the thing.
wrong.D: Variation among early sources concerns the period before specification and does not bear on its consequences.

questions.stem: The 'harder problem' the author identifies is:

choices.A: determining whether a surviving document is authentic
choices.B: the loss of documents to fire, flood and neglect
choices.C: the records that were never created in the first place
choices.D: the difficulty of reading documents in archaic languages

questions.explanation: The first paragraph sets up the standard scepticism, notes that it assumes 'the document exists', and names the harder problem as the one 'the training does not reach, because it concerns the documents that were never made'.

wrong.A: Authenticity is listed among the questions the training does cover.
wrong.B: The author's concern is with records never made, not with records made and then lost.
wrong.D: Language is never mentioned.

questions.stem: The examples of the manor and the colonial administration are offered to show that:

choices.A: archives over-represent economic activity relative to other kinds
choices.B: institutional purposes determine the shape of what survives
choices.C: medieval and colonial records are unusually unreliable
choices.D: record-keeping improved as institutions became more bureaucratic

questions.explanation: Both examples illustrate the paragraph's claim that an archive 'is the residue of institutions that kept records for their own purposes, and those purposes determined what was worth writing down'.

wrong.A: Economic activity happens to dominate these two examples, but the colonial case also covers punishment, and the general claim is about purposes rather than about economics.
wrong.C: Neither is singled out as unreliable; both are used as ordinary instances of how archives form.
wrong.D: No claim about improvement over time appears.

questions.stem: The author's criticism of reading against the grain is that it:

choices.A: recovers only what left some trace, while seeming to recover anything
choices.B: requires sources whose authors had no interest in the subject
choices.C: has been applied too rarely by historians of the colonial period
choices.D: depends on court records, which are unusually distorted

questions.explanation: The author calls the technique 'indispensable' and then gives its limit: it 'can only recover what left a trace in some record, however oblique', while the skilled practitioner 'may come to feel that nothing is beyond recovery'.

wrong.B: Oblique recording by uninterested authors is how the technique works, not an objection to it.
wrong.C: The author says nothing about how often it is used.
wrong.D: The brewing prosecution is offered as a successful example, not as a cautionary one.

questions.stem: A historian writes that villagers in a particular parish 'would have heard the sermon as a warning', citing no source for the claim. Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that the statement is:

choices.A: illegitimate, since no surviving document supports it
choices.B: acceptable only if the parish's records are unusually complete
choices.C: possibly the only route to a claim worth making, provided it is marked as inference
choices.D: testable by reading surviving sermons against the grain

questions.explanation: The passage grants that inference of this kind 'is sometimes the only route to a claim worth making' while warning that it 'produces an account that reads exactly like an account built from evidence'. The honest practice the author names is to mark the inference as what it is.

wrong.A: The author explicitly declines to rule such inference out, and says the temptation should be resisted in proportion to its usefulness rather than absolutely.
wrong.B: Completeness of the record is not the test the author proposes; the question is whether the inference is disclosed.
wrong.D: Reading against the grain recovers what left some oblique trace. A belief no institution had reason to record leaves no such trace, which is the limit the passage presses.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would place the LEAST confidence in which of the following historical claims?

choices.A: A particular manor collected a specified rent from its tenants in 1340
choices.B: Ordinary people in a medieval village held a particular view of the afterlife
choices.C: A colonial court convicted a specified number of people in a given year
choices.D: Women in a town brewed and sold ale in the fourteenth century

questions.explanation: The final paragraph draws exactly this contrast: a statement about rents rests on documents an institution 'had every reason to keep accurate', while a statement about belief rests on documents that mention belief 'incidentally, if at all'.

wrong.A: Rents are the author's own example of a well-founded claim.
wrong.C: Convictions are what a colonial administration recorded deliberately, so they are among the better-evidenced claims.
wrong.D: This is the author's example of a successful recovery by reading against the grain.

questions.stem: The author's closing point is that two historical statements written in the same tone:

choices.A: are equally likely to be true if both are supported by surviving documents
choices.B: may rest on evidence of very different strength, which the prose does not reveal
choices.C: should be rewritten so that the weaker one is expressed more tentatively
choices.D: cannot be compared, since they concern different kinds of subject

questions.explanation: The passage ends on precisely this: confidence 'depends on something the claim itself does not display', and the two statements 'may be written in the same tone, and should not be read in the same way'.

wrong.A: The author's whole point is that surviving support varies in strength depending on why the record was kept.
wrong.C: The closing instruction is addressed to the reader's reading, not to the historian's phrasing, though the author does commend marking inferences elsewhere.
wrong.D: The author compares them directly, so comparison is plainly possible.

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose is to:

choices.A: recover a better basis for a distinction that is usually drawn badly
choices.B: demonstrate that medieval pilgrimage was a commercial enterprise
choices.C: defend tourists against the condescension of travel writers
choices.D: argue that no useful distinction can be drawn between kinds of travel

questions.explanation: The passage dismantles the behavioural and inner-state versions of the distinction, then offers 'a more defensible version' located in the destination, and works out its consequence. The aim is relocation rather than demolition.

wrong.B: Commerce is evidence used against the behavioural version, not the object of the passage.
wrong.C: The author notes that the distinction 'flatters whoever is drawing it', but the argument is about where the distinction belongs, not about defending anyone.
wrong.D: The author explicitly offers a distinction they regard as real.

questions.stem: The author objects to locating the distinction in the traveller's inner state partly because:

choices.A: inner states cannot influence how a person travels
choices.B: it is harder to observe, which the author does not count in its favour
choices.C: medieval travellers left no record of their motives
choices.D: transformation is as common among tourists as diversion is among pilgrims

questions.explanation: The author's phrasing is exact: the inner-state version 'is harder to refute because it is harder to observe, which is not a point in its favour'. Unfalsifiability is treated as a weakness.

wrong.A: No such claim is made; the objection concerns observability and uniformity, not influence.
wrong.C: The passage reports several medieval motives, so records plainly exist.
wrong.D: The author gives examples on both sides but never asserts they occur at equal rates.

questions.stem: According to the author, the key feature of a shrine is that it:

choices.A: attracts travellers who have made a long journey
choices.B: has historically supported a commercial trade
choices.C: makes a claim on the visitor that the visitor may decline
choices.D: transforms those who stand in front of it

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph defines the distinction this way: a shrine 'asserts that something happened there which ought to alter the person standing in front of it', and a traveller 'may decline the shrine's claim, and many do'.

wrong.A: Distance travelled plays no part in the author's reframing.
wrong.B: Commerce surrounded shrines, but it is what the author uses to collapse the old distinction, not what defines a shrine.
wrong.D: The author is careful that the claim is made whether or not the visitor accepts it.

questions.stem: The final paragraph suggests that travel writers who prefer the original distinction would be unwelcome to learn that:

choices.A: battlefields and preserved camps attract more visitors than shrines do
choices.B: places they classify as touristic make the same claim shrines make
choices.C: pilgrims in shorts are as common as pilgrims in robes
choices.D: the inner-state version of the distinction cannot be observed

questions.explanation: The consequence the author draws is that 'many of the destinations they would class as touristic do make such claims', naming a battlefield, a camp and a writer's house. The flattering distinction collapses because the category the writers look down on contains the thing they prize.

wrong.A: No comparison of visitor numbers is made.
wrong.C: The clothing detail is colour in the argument rather than the finding.
wrong.D: That objection appears earlier and is not what the final paragraph adds.

questions.stem: Based on the author's reframing, which visit would NOT count as a pilgrimage?

choices.A: A traveller who visits a preserved concentration camp and leaves unmoved
choices.B: A traveller who visits a cathedral out of architectural interest
choices.C: A traveller who visits a beach and has a profound personal realisation there
choices.D: A traveller who visits a writer's house without having read the books

questions.explanation: On the author's account the distinction lies in the claim the place makes, not in what the visitor feels. A beach 'asserts nothing', so however transformed the visitor, the visit is not a pilgrimage in these terms.

wrong.A: The camp makes the claim; the author allows that a traveller 'may decline' it and many do, so the visit still counts.
wrong.B: A cathedral makes the claim regardless of why this visitor came.
wrong.D: A writer's house is named by the author as a site that makes such a claim.

questions.stem: The observation that a fourteenth-century traveller would find the modern tourist 'entirely legible' most directly undermines the view that:

choices.A: pilgrimage routes were commercially organised
choices.B: the two kinds of traveller differ in how they behave
choices.C: modern tourism has roots in religious practice
choices.D: souvenirs have always been mass-produced

questions.explanation: The comparison appears at the end of the paragraph documenting commerce, complaint, souvenirs and organised groups among pilgrims. Its work is to show that the behaviours said to mark the tourist were the pilgrim's behaviours too, which kills the behavioural version of the distinction.

wrong.A: The passage asserts this rather than undermining it.
wrong.C: Historical descent is not the author's claim; the point is similarity of behaviour, not lineage.
wrong.D: Badges and forged relics are described, but no claim about mass production in the medieval period is made.

questions.stem: The advocates' central claim about citizens' assemblies is that their recommendations:

choices.A: are more statistically representative than polling
choices.B: come from people who are accountable to the wider public
choices.C: are cheaper to obtain than other forms of consultation
choices.D: are better founded, reflecting what the public would think given time

questions.explanation: The second paragraph states the claim and rules out the alternative: not representativeness, but that the output is 'the view the public would hold if the public had the time'.

wrong.A: The author says advocates know a sample of forty is statistically worse than a poll of two thousand.
wrong.B: Accountability is raised by critics, and the author treats the members as answerable to nobody by design.
wrong.C: Cost appears only in the final line, as a criticism rather than an advocates' claim.

questions.stem: The author's conditional objection in the third paragraph is that the assembly's legitimacy:

choices.A: depends on features of the process that its audience cannot check
choices.B: disappears whenever a legislature declines to adopt the recommendation
choices.C: rests on a sample size too small to support any conclusion
choices.D: is undermined by paying participants for their time

questions.explanation: The paragraph ends on exactly this: 'The mechanism that gives the assembly its legitimacy is invisible to those who receive its output, which means the output cannot be assessed by its recipients.'

wrong.B: Non-adoption features in the author's reply to the accountability objection, not in this one.
wrong.C: The author grants the small sample and says representativeness is not the claim being made.
wrong.D: Payment is mentioned descriptively and never criticised.

questions.stem: The author considers the accountability objection weak because:

choices.A: members are selected at random and so cannot be captured by interests
choices.B: an assembly only proposes, while accountable bodies decide
choices.C: the facilitator is accountable even if the members are not
choices.D: accountability is less important than the quality of deliberation

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph argues that accountability matters for those who exercise continuing power, and that the assembly 'exercises no power at all unless a legislature adopts its recommendation'. 'The members propose; others dispose.'

wrong.A: Random selection is described but is not the author's reason for dismissing the objection.
wrong.C: The facilitator's accountability is never discussed.
wrong.D: The author never ranks the two; the argument is that the objection misapplies a standard.

questions.stem: A legislature refers a question it has repeatedly failed to settle to a citizens' assembly, then adopts the recommendation unchanged. According to the passage, the author's sharper worry about this would be that:

choices.A: the assembly's members were chosen by lot and answerable to nobody
choices.B: the experts who briefed the assembly may not have been balanced
choices.C: the recommendation may differ from what a poll of the population would have found
choices.D: the question is now difficult to oppose without appearing to oppose the public

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes the objections it answers from the one it presses. The sharper worry is that a question returns from an assembly 'difficult to oppose without appearing to oppose the public itself', so a procedure that makes a conclusion hard to argue with gets mistaken for one that makes it correct.

wrong.A: The author treats the accountability objection as weaker than it looks, since an assembly that dissolves exercises no power unless a legislature adopts its recommendation.
wrong.B: This is the author's conditional objection, raised earlier and distinguished from the sharper one.
wrong.C: The passage sets this aside at the start: advocates do not claim the assembly is more representative than a poll.

questions.stem: The author's statement that a procedure making a conclusion hard to argue with 'has not thereby made it correct' functions to:

choices.A: reject the use of citizens' assemblies on contested questions
choices.B: separate the persuasive force of a process from the truth of its output
choices.C: argue that legislatures should ignore assembly recommendations
choices.D: show that deliberation produces worse conclusions than polling

questions.explanation: The sentence distinguishes two things the passage has been circling: that an output is difficult to oppose, and that it is right. The author then warns against a democracy 'that cannot distinguish between the two'.

wrong.A: The author says the worry 'should give pause even to those sympathetic', which is caution rather than rejection.
wrong.C: No recommendation to legislatures is made; the author in fact relies on legislative adoption to answer the accountability objection.
wrong.D: The author accepts that deliberation produces better-founded opinions than a Tuesday-evening poll answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most strengthen the author's conditional objection?

choices.A: Assemblies have recommended policies that later proved unpopular
choices.B: Participants report finding the deliberation process rewarding
choices.C: Legislatures adopt assembly recommendations about half the time
choices.D: Reviews of expert panels found their composition shaped the conclusion reached

questions.explanation: The conditional objection is that the assembly's legitimacy depends on balance among experts and neutral facilitation, which the audience cannot verify. Evidence that panel composition actually determines the conclusion turns the hypothetical into a demonstrated risk.

wrong.A: Later unpopularity speaks to the recommendation's reception, not to whether the process was steered.
wrong.B: Participant satisfaction says nothing about whether the evidence they heard was balanced.
wrong.C: Adoption rates bear on the accountability objection the author already dismissed.

questions.stem: The 'difficulty' the author identifies in the standard definition is that:

choices.A: narrators rarely lie outright about events
choices.B: readers disagree about which details count as signals
choices.C: the evidence for doubting a narrator comes from the narrator
choices.D: the definition applies only to first-person narratives

questions.explanation: The first paragraph states it: 'in a first-person narrative there is nothing in the text that does not pass through the narrator', so 'the reader who concludes that a narrator is lying has done so using evidence the liar supplied'.

wrong.A: The frequency of outright lying is never discussed.
wrong.B: Reader disagreement appears later as a consequence, not as the difficulty in the definition.
wrong.D: The author confines the discussion to first-person narration without treating that as the problem.

questions.stem: The claim that 'a signal that is missed is not a signal' supports the author's view that unreliability is:

choices.A: a relation between a text and a particular reader
choices.B: a technique that only skilled authors can execute
choices.C: more common in modern fiction than in earlier periods
choices.D: detectable by careful attention to the surrounding facts

questions.explanation: The sentence leads directly to the conclusion: unreliability is 'not a property of a text but a relation between a text and a reader', with the same novel reading differently for different readers.

wrong.B: Authorial skill is not the subject; the author's point is about reception.
wrong.C: No historical comparison is offered.
wrong.D: Attention to surrounding facts is the technique being described, and the author's point is that it may fail.

questions.stem: The author objects to critics who appeal to authorial intention because such an appeal:

choices.A: cannot be verified for authors who are no longer living
choices.B: leaves the text for something outside it, which those critics reject elsewhere
choices.C: assumes that authors always know what they have written
choices.D: makes every reading equally defensible

questions.explanation: The third paragraph calls it 'a retreat from the text to something outside it, and one that most of the same critics would refuse in other arguments'. The charge is inconsistency.

wrong.A: Verification is not the complaint, and the author says nothing about living authors.
wrong.C: Authors' self-knowledge is not discussed.
wrong.D: That is closer to what the author's own position must answer, not to the objection raised here.

questions.stem: On the author's account, one reading of a novel is better than another when it:

choices.A: accords with what the author is known to have intended
choices.B: is held by the greater number of qualified critics
choices.C: makes more of the book significant
choices.D: requires fewer assumptions about the narrator's motives

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph gives the test directly: a reading is defended 'by showing what it makes available', and 'a reading that illuminates more of the book is better than one that illuminates less'.

wrong.A: Intention is the retreat the author has just rejected.
wrong.B: Critical consensus is never offered as a standard.
wrong.D: Economy of assumption is not the criterion proposed.

questions.stem: The author introduces the hard case of the narrator who murders someone in order to:

choices.A: concede that the proposed test breaks down in extreme cases
choices.B: show that the test still discriminates where it is most doubted
choices.C: argue that some novels have only one defensible reading
choices.D: illustrate why critics prefer appeals to intention

questions.explanation: The author raises the case as the objection a reader will feel most strongly - 'it is another to say' - and then answers it: 'the test survives the hard case', because the reading in which nothing happened 'leaves a great deal of the book inert'.

wrong.A: The author says the opposite: the test survives.
wrong.C: The conclusion is that one reading fails as a reading, which leaves the plural framework intact rather than reducing the novel to a single reading.
wrong.D: Intention was dealt with in the previous paragraph and is not the point of the hard case.
